paper_name: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945–1995

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: Territorial changes and their impact after 1948-49 war
questions.question_text: Explain two distinct consequences of the border and territorial shifts produced by the 1948–49 Arab-Israeli War.
indicative_content: Israel expanded its territory by 21% beyond the UN partition borders, securing control of Western Galilee, the coastal plain, and West Jerusalem.

The remainder of Arab Palestine was absorbed: Jordan annexed the West Bank and East Jerusalem, while Egypt occupied the Gaza Strip, leaving no independent Palestinian state and creating 700,000 refugees.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain two distinct consequences with specific historical detail (e.g. 21% land increase; Jordanian annexation of West Bank).

questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: Israel and Egypt, 1973-79: Sadat, peace initiative, Camp David
questions.question_text: Construct an analytical narrative tracing how relations between Egypt and Israel evolved from 1973 to 1977.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: outbreak and outcome of the October 1973 Yom Kippur War
• Optional focus: President Anwar Sadat’s diplomatic pivot and Knesset visit
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: The Yom Kippur War (1973) broke the myth of Israeli invincibility and restored Arab pride, giving Sadat the political standing to negotiate from strength.
US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger initiated "shuttle diplomacy", leading to the 1974 and 1975 Sinai Disengagement Agreements where Israel withdrew from the Suez Canal and returned oil fields.
Sadat made a historic visit to Jerusalem in November 1977, addressing the Knesset in person and opening direct peace negotiations.
questions.examiner_tips: Structure chronologically with explicit causal linking phrases ("This led to", "As a consequence", "Following this breakthrough").

questions.topic: Nasser: Leadership of the Arab World
questions.spec_topic: KT1.3: Nasser and Egypt’s leadership of the Arab world
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of Gamal Abdel Nasser in shaping leadership and pan-Arab nationalism across the Arab world.
indicative_content: Nasser championed Pan-Arab nationalism and anti-imperialism, inspiring Arab nations by nationalising the Suez Canal (1956) and standing up to Britain, France, and Israel.
His leadership led to the creation of the United Arab Republic (UAR, 1958) uniting Egypt and Syria, and made Egypt the undisputed diplomatic and military champion of the Palestinian cause.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain the impact on Arab unity, opposition to Western imperialism, and the escalating conflict with Israel.

questions.topic: Occupied Territories After Six Day War (1967)
questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: Aftermath of the 1967 war: Sinai, Gaza, West Bank, Golan Heights, Jerusalem
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of Israel’s capture of the Occupied Territories in June 1967 for subsequent Arab-Israeli relations.
indicative_content: Israel gained strategic depth and security buffers by capturing the Sinai, Gaza Strip, West Bank, Golan Heights, and East Jerusalem.
It hardened Arab hostility, leading to the Arab League’s "Three No’s" at Khartoum (No peace, no recognition, no negotiations) and brought 1 million Palestinians under Israeli military occupation.
questions.examiner_tips: Evaluate how capturing the territories created both security buffers for Israel and permanent diplomatic deadlock.

questions.topic: End of Cold War & Middle East Peace
questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Attempts to find a solution: end of Cold War, Madrid Conference 1991
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of the collapse of Soviet power and the end of the Cold War for Middle East peace diplomacy.
indicative_content: The collapse of the USSR left the USA as the sole global superpower and cut off Soviet military and financial backing for Syria and the PLO.
Deprived of Soviet support, Arab nations and the PLO were forced to negotiate directly with Israel, paving the way for the Madrid Conference (1991) and the Oslo peace process.
questions.examiner_tips: Focus on superpower balance of power shifting and forcing Arab states towards diplomatic negotiation.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: The Oslo Accords (1993): terms and impact
questions.question_text: Explain two distinct consequences of signing the 1993 Oslo I Accord (Declaration of Principles).
indicative_content: Mutual recognition: Israel recognized the PLO as the legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, and the PLO renounced terrorism and recognized Israel’s right to exist.

Creation of the Palestinian National Authority (PNA) with limited self-rule over parts of the Gaza Strip and West Bank (Jericho), though final status issues (Jerusalem, refugees, borders) were postponed.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain two distinct consequences: mutual recognition and the establishment of the Palestinian Authority.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.3: Events and significance of the Suez Crisis (1956)
questions.question_text: Construct an analytical narrative tracing the causes, course, and outcome of the 1956 Suez Crisis.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Nasser’s nationalisation of the Suez Canal Company (July 1956)
• Optional focus: Anglo-French and Israeli military intervention (Protocol of Sèvres)
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in July 1956 after the US and UK withdrew funding for the Aswan High Dam.
Britain, France, and Israel held secret talks at Sèvres, agreeing Israel would invade the Sinai Peninsula and Britain/France would intervene as "peacekeepers" to seize the canal.

Israel invaded on 29 October; British and French paratroopers landed on 5 November, but intense US diplomatic and financial pressure (threatening to collapse the British pound) forced a humiliating withdrawal.
questions.examiner_tips: Sequence the events chronologically: nationalisation -> Sèvres collusion -> military invasion -> US intervention and withdrawal.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: Creation of the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF)
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of forming the unified Israel Defense Forces (IDF) in 1948 for securing the newborn Israeli state.
indicative_content: Unified command: David Ben-Gurion dissolved rival paramilitary factions (Haganah, Irgun, Lehi) into a single national military under state control.
It established universal military conscription and a doctrine of rapid mobilization and pre-emptive attack that ensured survival in 1948-49 and subsequent conflicts.
questions.examiner_tips: Highlight the removal of factional militias and the creation of an organized, disciplined national army.

questions.topic: Superpowers and the Outbreak of 1967 War
questions.spec_topic: KT2.1: The actions of the USSR, Nasser and the USA leading to Six Day War
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of Soviet and American policies in escalating the crisis that triggered the June 1967 Six-Day War.
indicative_content: The USSR provided false intelligence to Syria and Egypt that Israel was massing troops on the Syrian border, prompting Nasser to mobilize in the Sinai and expel the UNEF.
The USA provided political and covert intelligence support to Israel, signaling that Washington would not oppose an Israeli pre-emptive strike if Egyptian forces closed the Straits of Tiran.
questions.examiner_tips: Analyse Soviet false intelligence and American tacit approval of Israel’s pre-emptive strike.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2 & KT3.1: Expulsion from Jordan, PLO in Lebanon, Israeli security
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of PLO cross-border operations from southern Lebanon (1970–82) for Israel’s security policy.
indicative_content: After expulsion from Jordan in Black September (1970), the PLO established "Fatahland" in southern Lebanon, launching cross-border rocket attacks and terrorist raids into northern Israel.

This forced Israel to launch Operation Litani (1978) and the full-scale 1982 invasion of Lebanon (Operation Peace for Galilee), leading to the Siege of Beirut and the expulsion of the PLO leadership to Tunisia.
questions.examiner_tips: Link PLO cross-border rocket attacks directly to Israel’s military invasions of southern Lebanon in 1978 and 1982.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.1: The First Intifada: causes, course and consequences
questions.question_text: Explain two distinct consequences of the First Palestinian Intifada (1987–93).
indicative_content: International sympathy shifted towards Palestinians as global media broadcast images of teenage stone-throwers facing heavily armed Israeli soldiers (the "Iron Fist" policy).
It convinced Israeli leaders (Yitzhak Rabin) that military occupation was unsustainable and pushed the PLO towards diplomacy, paving the way for the 1993 Oslo Peace Process.
questions.examiner_tips: Focus on the shift in international public opinion and the realization that a political rather than military solution was required.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: The use of terrorism: PFLP airplane hijacks 1970; Munich Olympics 1972
questions.question_text: Construct an analytical narrative tracing key events in the Palestinian armed struggle between 1970 and 1972.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: PFLP Dawson’s Field hijackings and Black September in Jordan (1970)
• Optional focus: the Munich Olympics hostage crisis (September 1972)
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: In September 1970, the PFLP hijacked four international airliners and flew three to Dawson’s Field in Jordan, blowing up the empty planes on live television.
King Hussein of Jordan launched Black September (1970), defeating and expelling the PLO from Jordan to Lebanon.

In September 1972, Black September terrorists infiltrated the Munich Olympic village, taking 11 Israeli athletes hostage; all 11 were murdered during a botched German rescue operation, provoking Israel’s "Operation Wrath of God" assassination campaign.
questions.examiner_tips: Show how Dawson’s Field caused the expulsion from Jordan, which in turn spawned Black September and the Munich massacre.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.1: Partition and UN Resolution 181
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of the November 1947 UN Partition Plan (Resolution 181) in bringing about the State of Israel.
indicative_content: It provided international legitimacy by recommending the partition of Palestine into independent Jewish and Arab states with Jerusalem as an international corpus separatum.
It was accepted by the Jewish Agency but rejected by Arab states, triggering the 1947-48 civil war in Mandatory Palestine and the 1948 Arab-Israeli War upon British withdrawal.
questions.examiner_tips: Emphasise legal international recognition alongside immediate Arab rejection and the outbreak of fighting.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The Law of Return (1950) and immigration
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of the 1950 Law of Return for Israel’s demographic, economic, and military growth.
indicative_content: It granted every Jewish person anywhere in the world the legal right to settle in Israel and gain immediate citizenship.
It led to massive mass immigration (doubling the Jewish population from 650,000 to 1.3 million within four years), providing crucial manpower for the economy and the IDF.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain both the demographic doubling of Israel’s population and the economic/military strengthening of the state.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: Israel and Egypt: Kissinger’s shuttle diplomacy and disengagement agreements
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of Henry Kissinger’s 1973–75 shuttle diplomacy in advancing Arab-Israeli disengagement talks.
indicative_content: US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger flew back and forth between Cairo, Jerusalem, and Damascus to negotiate separate bilateral disengagement pacts.
It defused the immediate post-Yom Kippur military confrontation, secured Israeli troop withdrawals in the Sinai and Golan, and proved peaceful compromise was possible between Arabs and Israelis.
questions.examiner_tips: Focus on how bilateral agreements separated Egypt from the broader Arab rejectionist front.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.1: Syria’s support for Fatah and escalating tension
questions.question_text: Explain two distinct consequences of Syrian backing for Fatah guerrilla raids between 1964 and 1967.
indicative_content: Syria allowed Fatah guerrillas to launch armed sabotage raids into northern Israel from Syrian territory, leading to violent Israeli retaliatory strikes (e.g. the dogfight of 7 April 1967 where Israel shot down six Syrian MiGs).
It escalated regional tensions and prompted Egypt and Syria to sign a mutual defence pact in November 1966, pulling Nasser inexorably into conflict with Israel.
questions.examiner_tips: State two distinct consequences: cross-border retaliation and the Egyptian-Syrian mutual defence alliance.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Oslo Accords, Oslo II (1995), assassination of Rabin
questions.question_text: Construct an analytical narrative tracing Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations from the 1993 Oslo talks to Oslo II in 1995.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Yasser Arafat, Yitzhak Rabin, and mutual recognition letters (1993)
• Optional focus: West Bank Areas A, B, and C under the Oslo II Accord (1995)
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Secret negotiations in Norway led to the signing of the Oslo Accords (Declaration of Principles) in Washington on 13 September 1993, with the famous handshake between Rabin and Arafat.
In May 1994, the Gaza-Jericho Agreement implemented Palestinian self-rule, and Yasser Arafat returned from exile to head the newly formed Palestinian Authority.
Oslo II (1995) divided the West Bank into Areas A, B, and C; however, growing extremism culminated in the assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin by an Israeli extremist in November 1995.
questions.examiner_tips: Structure chronologically: Oslo I (1993) -> Gaza-Jericho (1994) -> Oslo II (1995) -> Rabin’s assassination.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: Refugee status of Palestinian Arabs
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of the 1948–49 territorial partition and armistice lines for Palestinian Arab society and refugees.
indicative_content: The Nakba ("Catastrophe"): over 700,000 Palestinian Arabs became refugees, displaced from their homes into squalid camps in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Syria, and Lebanon.
Arab Palestine ceased to exist as a political entity: Gaza fell under Egyptian military administration, while the West Bank and East Jerusalem were annexed by Jordan.
questions.examiner_tips: Analyse the humanitarian refugee crisis and the total loss of territorial self-determination.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: PFLP airplane hijacks of 1970 and international attitudes
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of the September 1970 PFLP airliner hijackings in shaping global perceptions of the Palestinian cause.
indicative_content: The dramatic destruction of three jetliners at Dawson’s Field thrust the Palestinian cause onto global front pages and television screens.
While it publicized Palestinian statelessness, it also led Western nations to brand Palestinian nationalist organizations as dangerous international terrorists.
questions.examiner_tips: Address the dual impact: massive global visibility balanced against the stigma of international air piracy.

questions.topic: Yom Kippur War (1973) for Israel-Egypt Relations
questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: Yom Kippur War, Sadat, diplomacy
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of the October 1973 Yom Kippur War in transforming diplomatic relations between Israel and Egypt.
indicative_content: Egypt’s successful crossing of the Bar-Lev Line shattered Israeli assumptions of permanent military invulnerability and restored Egyptian national honour.
It convinced both sides that military force could not resolve the conflict, opening the door for Henry Kissinger’s disengagement agreements and ultimately Sadat’s peace treaty.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain why military stalemate created the necessary psychological preconditions for peace talks.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: Black September and the Munich Olympics (1972)
questions.question_text: Explain two distinct consequences of Black September’s attack at the 1972 Munich Olympic Games.
indicative_content: Israel launched "Operation Wrath of God", a covert Mossad assassination campaign hunting down and assassinating Black September leaders and planners across Europe.
Israel launched retaliatory airstrikes against Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon and Syria, killing scores of civilians and militants.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain Mossad’s assassination campaign and massive retaliatory air strikes into Lebanon and Syria.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: Territorial consolidation, Law of Return, IDF, US aid
questions.question_text: Construct an analytical narrative tracing how the new State of Israel consolidated itself between 1949 and 1954.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: defending the 1949 Green Line armistice borders
• Optional focus: building the IDF, absorbing Jewish immigrants, and foreign aid
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Following armistice agreements in 1949, Israel consolidated control over its expanded borders and began building agricultural kibbutzim and border defences.
The Law of Return (1950) triggered unprecedented immigration from post-Holocaust Europe and Arab countries, doubling the population.
To defend this population, the IDF was professionalized into a modern citizen army, backed by substantial US financial loans and German Holocaust reparations.
questions.examiner_tips: Structure: Armistice consolidation -> immigration wave under Law of Return -> IDF strengthening and US aid.

questions.topic: Conflicting Interests of Jews & Arabs in Mandate
questions.spec_topic: KT1.1: Conflicting interests and demands of Jews and Arabs in British Mandate
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of irreconcilable Jewish and Arab aims in forcing Britain to surrender the Palestine Mandate.
indicative_content: Zionists demanded unrestricted immigration and an independent Jewish homeland, while Arab leaders demanded an end to Jewish land purchases and an independent Arab-majority state.

The conflicting demands resulted in violent Jewish insurgencies against British rule (bombing of King David Hotel 1946), making Palestine ungovernable and forcing Britain to hand the problem to the UN in 1947.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain how irreconcilable national demands made Britain’s mandate completely untenable.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: The oil crisis (1973-74) and international diplomacy
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of the 1973–74 OAPEC oil embargo in accelerating US-led Middle East diplomacy.
indicative_content: OPEC Arab oil producers weaponised oil, imposing an embargo on the US and the Netherlands and quadrupling global oil prices.
This caused severe Western inflation and forced the US and Western European governments to adopt a much more active, balanced diplomatic role in pressuring Israel to negotiate.
questions.examiner_tips: Analyse how the oil shock forced Western powers to push Israel into diplomatic disengagement.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.1: The Israeli invasion of Lebanon (1982) and its impact
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of Israel’s June 1982 invasion of Lebanon (Operation Peace for Galilee) for the PLO and Palestinians.
indicative_content: Operation Peace for Galilee besieged Beirut, forcing the PLO and Yasser Arafat to evacuate to distant exile in Tunisia, weakening their direct military threat.
The Sabra and Shatila massacre of Palestinian refugees by Christian Phalangist allies provoked international outrage and widespread domestic protests inside Israel.
questions.examiner_tips: Address the expulsion of the PLO leadership to Tunisia and the international shock of the Sabra and Shatila massacres.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: Sadat’s visit to Israel (1977) and Camp David Accords
questions.question_text: Explain two distinct consequences of Egyptian President Anwar Sadat’s November 1977 mission to Jerusalem.
indicative_content: It broke decades of diplomatic taboo by addressing the Israeli Knesset in person, leading directly to the Camp David Accords (1978) and the Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty (1979).
Egypt was ostracized by the Arab world, expelled from the Arab League, and Sadat was branded a traitor by Arab militants, ultimately leading to his assassination in 1981.
questions.examiner_tips: Highlight the positive breakthrough with Israel (Camp David) and the severe Arab backlash against Egypt.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2 & KT1.3: Relations with Egypt, Farouk, Nasser, Gaza raid, Suez
questions.question_text: Construct an analytical narrative tracing the worsening confrontation between Israel and Egypt from 1949 to 1956.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: the 1952 Free Officers’ coup removing King Farouk
• Optional focus: Gaza raids, Czech arms, and the Suez Canal crisis
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Following the 1949 armistice, Egypt maintained border tensions and blockaded the Straits of Tiran and Suez Canal to Israeli shipping.

The 1952 Free Officers revolution overthrew King Farouk, bringing Gamal Abdel Nasser to power with a militant anti-Zionist foreign policy; fedayeen guerrilla raids triggered the bloody Israeli Gaza Raid (1955).
Nasser secured Soviet weapons in the Czech Arms Deal (1955) and nationalized the Suez Canal in July 1956, prompting the joint Israeli, British, and French military attack in October 1956.
questions.examiner_tips: Narrate the chain: 1949 border friction -> 1952 Free Officers -> 1955 Gaza Raid and arms deal -> 1956 Suez War.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.1: End of the British Mandate and creation of Israel
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of Britain’s withdrawal from Mandatory Palestine in May 1948 for the establishment of Israel.
indicative_content: The British withdrawal on 14 May 1948 allowed David Ben-Gurion to formally declare the establishment of the State of Israel.
It removed British military presence that had maintained order, triggering the immediate invasion of Israel by five Arab armies on 15 May 1948.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain how the British departure created the legal power vacuum that enabled the Israeli declaration of statehood.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: UN Resolution 242 and "land for peace"
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of UN Security Council Resolution 242 (November 1967) for diplomacy between Israel and neighbouring Arab states.
indicative_content: It established the fundamental "land for peace" formula, requiring Israeli withdrawal from territories occupied in the recent conflict in exchange for Arab recognition of Israel’s secure borders.
Ambiguities in the English versus French texts ("from territories" vs "from the territories") allowed both sides to dispute the scope of withdrawal, stalling peace for years.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain the "land for peace" principle and the diplomatic ambiguity over which territories were included.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Arafat’s declaration (1988), recognition of Israel
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of Yasser Arafat’s December 1988 renunciation of terrorism and acceptance of two states for peace talks.
indicative_content: In December 1988, Yasser Arafat accepted UN Resolutions 242 and 338, renounced all forms of terrorism, and recognized Israel’s right to exist in peace.
This met long-standing US conditions, allowing the United States to open direct diplomatic dialogue with the PLO and setting the diplomatic stage for the Madrid and Oslo peace conferences.
questions.examiner_tips: Focus on how renouncing terrorism made the PLO an acceptable diplomatic negotiating partner for the USA.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.1: Significance of the bombing of the King David Hotel (1946)
questions.question_text: Explain one distinct consequence of the July 1946 Irgun bombing of British headquarters at the King David Hotel.
indicative_content: The Irgun’s bombing destroyed British military and civil headquarters, killing 91 people, shocking British public opinion and convincing the British government that policing the Mandate was too costly in lives and money, accelerating Britain’s decision to hand Palestine to the UN.
questions.examiner_tips: Highlight the collapse of British domestic political will to stay in Palestine.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: Territorial changes and aftermath of 1948-49 war
questions.question_text: Explain one distinct consequence of the 1949 armistice border changes after the First Arab-Israeli War.
indicative_content: Israel secured 78% of Mandatory Palestine (an increase of 21% beyond the UN partition plan), establishing a continuous, defensible land corridor to West Jerusalem, while leaving no independent Palestinian Arab state.
questions.examiner_tips: Focus on Israeli territorial expansion and the division of Jerusalem into Jewish West and Jordanian East.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2 & KT3.1: Expulsion from Jordan, PLO in Lebanon, Israeli security, 1982 war
questions.question_text: Construct an analytical narrative tracing the PLO’s presence in Lebanon and escalating conflict with Israel between 1970 and 1982.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: PLO relocation to Beirut after Black September in Jordan (1970)
• Optional focus: cross-border raids, Operation Litani, and the 1982 Israeli invasion
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: After expulsion from Jordan during Black September (1970), the PLO re-established its military bases and headquarters in southern Lebanon and West Beirut.
From southern Lebanon, the PLO launched cross-border Katyusha rocket attacks and guerrilla raids into northern Israel, provoking Israeli counter-strikes and Operation Litani in 1978.
In June 1982, Israel launched Operation Peace for Galilee, besieging Beirut and forcing Yasser Arafat and thousands of PLO fighters to evacuate Lebanon for exile in Tunisia.
questions.examiner_tips: Structure chronologically: Black September -> southern Lebanon cross-border raids -> 1982 Israeli invasion and evacuation to Tunisia.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.3: Nasser and Egypt’s leadership: Gaza 1955, Suez 1956, UAR 1958
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of President Nasser’s policies in heightening regional Middle East tensions between 1955 and 1963.
indicative_content: Nasser escalated conflict with Israel by purchasing Soviet arms in 1955 and nationalising the Suez Canal in 1956, leading directly to the Suez Crisis.
His Pan-Arab leadership and formation of the United Arab Republic (UAR) in 1958 surrounded Israel with hostile rhetoric and heightened border clashes.
questions.examiner_tips: Link Nasser’s anti-imperialist rhetoric, Soviet arms, and the UAR to rising regional insecurity.

questions.topic: Six Day War (1967) for Israel’s Security
questions.spec_topic: KT2.1 & KT2.2: Six Day War and aftermath for Israel’s security
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of Israel’s victory in the June 1967 Six-Day War for its strategic border security.
indicative_content: Israel destroyed Egyptian, Syrian, and Jordanian air forces within hours, eliminating the immediate threat of annihilation and establishing regional air supremacy.
Capturing the Sinai, Golan Heights, and West Bank created massive geographic buffer zones, putting major Israeli cities out of direct artillery range.
questions.examiner_tips: Address both the immediate destruction of hostile air forces and the acquisition of geographic buffer zones.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Israel-Jordan peace treaty (1994)
questions.question_text: Analyse the significance of the October 1994 Israel-Jordan Peace Treaty in advancing regional Middle East peace.
indicative_content: Jordan became only the second Arab state to formally recognize Israel and sign a full peace treaty, securing Israel’s longest land border.
It resolved water rights, established security cooperation, and reinforced momentum from the Oslo Accords, demonstrating regional normalization was viable.
questions.examiner_tips: Highlight the stabilization of Israel’s eastern border and the momentum it lent to regional diplomacy.
